title.narrative: OXFAM Climate Adaptation for Rural Livelihoods Phase 2 (CARL 2) 2022- 2025
OXFAM Climate Adaptation for Rural Livelihoods Phase 2 (CARL 2) 2022- 2025

description.narrative:
The Climate Adaptation for Rural Livelihoods programme expects to achieve:
1. Increased climate-smart agricultural solutions, technology and innovation integrated with natural resource management, biodiversity protection and diversified livelihoods at the household and landscape level.
Activities include targeted awareness raising for 20 000 beneficiaries on natural resource management and biodiversity conservation and capacity building on adaptation at sub national level structures. There is also support for concrete, context specific resilient building measures to be adopted at household, community and landscape level including a large wetland fencing and agroforestry component and focus on regenerative soil fertility management, soil moisture conservation and rainwater harvesting.
2. Increased women and youth economic empowerment and more equitable access and control over household and community resources.
Activities include training and support for linking women and youth to appropriate, climate smart, high value chains, providing catalyst funding for women and youth entrepreneurs and policy briefs developed on unfair trading practices in targeted value chains.
3. Enhanced hydro-meteorological products, dissemination, and use.
Activities include quality control mechanisms established to improve data management, developing appropriate meteorological products to improve forecasting, and improving dissemination and accessibility of the forecasts and early weather warnings.
The project vision is that of a resilient rural Zimbabwe, where poor, vulnerable and rural communities and institutions are able to anticipate, adapt and respond to climate shocks and other stresses, take charge of their own inclusive development while sustainably managing diverse natural resources and valuing biodiversity.

Insatsen "Climate Adaptation for Rural Livelihoods" förväntas öka inkomster för personer som lever i fattigdom på landsbygden, förbättra jordbruksproduktivitet och klimatresiliens samt förbättra förvaltning av naturresurser och skydda och återställa den biologiska mångfalden.
Insatsen mål är att 1) Öka antalet klimatsmarta lösningar inom jordbruket som integreras med naturresursförvaltning, skydd av biologisk mångfald samt diversifierad försörjning på hushålls- och landskapsnivå , 2) Stärka kvinnors och ungdomars ekonomiska egenmakt samt en mer jämlik tillgång till och kontroll över hushållets och gemensamma resurser, 3) Förbättra hydrometeorologiska produkter samt deras spridning och användning.
Insatsen förväntas bidra till SDG-målen 1, 2, 5, 13 och 15.

The Climate Adaptation for Rural Livelihoods programme is expected to increase incomes for the rural poor, improve agricultural productivity and climate resilience and improve management of natural resources and protect and restore biodiversity. The objectives are to 1. Increase climate-smart agricultural solutions, technology and innovation integrated with natural resource management, biodiversity protection and diversified livelihoods at the household and landscape level. 2. Increase women and youth economic empowerment and more equitable access and control over household and community resources. 3. Enhance hydro meteorological products, dissemination and use. The programme will contribute towards SDGs 1,2,5,13 and 15.

The project successfully executed its core mandate by scaling up adaptation measures rooted in the foodclimatenatural resourcesbiodiversity nexus. It also managed to exceed its targets, ultimately supporting over 20,00 vulnerable households located in four climatestressed districts: Buhera, Gutu, Bulilima and Mberengwa. By combining food security, advanced gender justice and promoting environmentally sustainable rural livelihoods, the resilience among the beneficaries could be strenghtened. The project reached 23,641 households (against a target of 20,000) and an estimated 118,205 indirect beneficiaries, including 46 persons with disabilities. The overall resilience index across the four districts averaged approximately 61%, indicating that these households have capacities to moderate drought shocks which reflect meaningful progress in resiliencebuilding. Main project progress towards outcomes Outcome 1: Adaptive Knowledge and Practice Outcome 1 sought to strengthen the knowledge base and raise awareness of local institutions, stakeholders and smallholder farmers on climate change, natural resources management, biodiversity conservation and gender transformative Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA). This was done by utilizing a variety of methods such as facetoface farmer training, field days and Farmer Field Schools (FFS) to mention a few. The project managed to convert climate awareness into the widespread adoption of resilient practices. The adoption rate for CSA practices reached 94 %, which significantly surpasses the 35 % target increase, following awareness training provided to 22,787 individuals. Sustainable Natural Resource Management (SNRM) practices reached 81% adoption which conserved 23,446.7 hectares of land. Additionally, nine wetlands were restored. Livelihood diversification reached 76 % of households, providing new income streams through small livestock, value addition, horticulture, apiculture, aquaculture, Village Savings and Lending Associations (VSLAs), petty trading and microenterprises. Small livestock initiatives benefited 1,839 households. This was achieved, for example, through increases in average goat prices and poultry interventions targeting chickens and improved egg sales. Furthermore, water security and water access improved through 21 solarized micro irrigations schemes (18 new and 3 rehabilitated), covering 142 hectares and thus benefiting 1,234 households. In addition, borehole expansion resulted in the drilling and rehabilitation of 64 boreholes in total. 6,341 households directly benefited from this critical infrastructure and agricultural productivity was boosted. Value chains such as goats, honey, sorghum, horticulture, cowpeas, sugar beans and poultry were strengthened. Agroforestry initiatives planted 9,552 fruit trees, benefiting 1,785 farmers. The project used integrated micro watershed management, VSLAs, FFS, CSAs, value chains development, the biodiversity wheel, NBS and asset creation/strengthening as approaches and methods to reach outcome 1. Outcome 2: Economic & Gender Empowerment Outcome 2 focused on the enhanced economic empowerment of women and youth through improved access to and control over household and community resources. 15,599 women and youth were reached by the CARL 2 project, surpassing its target of 6,000. It catalyzed economic empowerment with 1,476 new businesses launched in poultry, fish farming, petty trade, honey processing and goat production. Leadership transformation was evident as 689 women assumed roles in community governance structures, including irrigation committees and climate resilience platforms. Massive results were achieved in poverty reduction and gender equity by positioning women and youth in the center of economic decisionmaking processes. The support led to a consistent upward trajectory in household incomes. For instance, average household income increased sharply from 23 USD to 190 USD in one district by Year 3. Up to 96% of households reported improved ownership and control of assets. These resiliencebuilding interventions exhibit how targeted support enabled women, youth and households to shift from a position of vulnerability to one of agency, thereby fostering inclusive economic empowerment and climate resilience. Outcome 3: Enhanced Early Warning Systems Outcome 3 aimed to strengthen the capacity of national hydrometeorological services to generate, disseminate and promote the use of improved hydrometeorological products under CARL 2. By capacitating the Meteorological Services Department (MSD), University of Zimbabwe and Zimbabwe National Water Authority (ZINWA), tailored training, mentorship, coaching and userneeds workshops could be arranged. Together with SMHI, Oxfam also facilitated four SMHI technical missions to Zimbabwe and an organized study visit to Sweden for 12 hydromet professionals. The project transformed how farmers access and utilize critical weather information, thereby strengthening their capacity to manage climaterelated risk. Access to climate and early warning information was expanded to a total of 28,128 women and youth and by the end of the project Zimbabwes hydrometeorological services were strengthened through multiple localization efforts such as meteograms. The average farmer satisfaction rate with the quality of the information reached a remarkable 95% by Year 3.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
